    OPT   Est. Local Speedup: 42.6%                                                                                     
          Every scheduler is capable of issuing one instruction per cycle, but for this workload each scheduler only    
          issues an instruction every 2.2 cycles. This might leave hardware resources underutilized and may lead to     
          less optimal performance. Out of the maximum of 12 warps per scheduler, this workload allocates an average    
          of 10.92 active warps per scheduler, but only an average of 0.93 warps were eligible per cycle. Eligible      
          warps are the subset of active warps that are ready to issue their next instruction. Every cycle with no      
          eligible warp results in no instruction being issued and the issue slot remains unused. To increase the       
          number of eligible warps, avoid possible load imbalances due to highly different execution durations per      
          warp. Reducing stalls indicated on the Warp State Statistics and Source Counters sections can help, too.

    OPT   Est. Speedup: 12.35%                                                                                          
          Instructions are executed in warps, which are groups of 32 threads. Optimal instruction throughput is         
          achieved if all 32 threads of a warp execute the same instruction. The chosen launch configuration, early     
          thread completion, and divergent flow control can significantly lower the number of active threads in a warp  
          per cycle. This workload achieves an average of 25.0 threads being active per cycle. This is further reduced  
          to 22.9 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.      
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

    Section: Scheduler Statistics
    ---------------------------- ----------- ------------
    Metric Name                  Metric Unit Metric Value
    ---------------------------- ----------- ------------
    One or More Eligible                   %         4.60
    Issued Warp Per Scheduler                        0.05
    No Eligible                            %        95.40
    Active Warps Per Scheduler          warp         2.72
    Eligible Warps Per Scheduler        warp         0.07
    ---------------------------- ----------- ------------

    OPT   Est. Local Speedup: 52.52%                                                                                    
          Every scheduler is capable of issuing one instruction per cycle, but for this workload each scheduler only    
          issues an instruction every 21.8 cycles. This might leave hardware resources underutilized and may lead to    
          less optimal performance. Out of the maximum of 12 warps per scheduler, this workload allocates an average    
          of 2.72 active warps per scheduler, but only an average of 0.07 warps were eligible per cycle. Eligible       
          warps are the subset of active warps that are ready to issue their next instruction. Every cycle with no      
          eligible warp results in no instruction being issued and the issue slot remains unused. To increase the       
          number of eligible warps, reduce the time the active warps are stalled by inspecting the top stall reasons    
          on the Warp State Statistics and Source Counters sections.

    OPT   Est. Speedup: 32.98%                                                                                          
          This workload accesses local memory                                                                           
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          57.43% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each       
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.

          This workload accesses local memory                                                                           
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          3.52% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each        
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.                                                      
          14.12% of all local loads and 98.70% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 18.72% of    
          all sectors requested in L2.                                                                                  
          One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being    
          indexed using compile time constants (see the "Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide            
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice    
          on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation

          less optimal performance. Out of the maximum of 12 warps per scheduler, this workload allocates an average    
          of 11.22 active warps per scheduler, but only an average of 1.20 warps were eligible per cycle. Eligible      
          warps are the subset of active warps that are ready to issue their next instruction. Every cycle with no      
          eligible warp results in no instruction being issued and the issue slot remains unused. To increase the       
          number of eligible warps, avoid possible load imbalances due to highly different execution durations per      
          warp. Reducing stalls indicated on the Warp State Statistics and Source Counters sections can help, too.

          This workload accesses local memory                                                                           
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          57.25% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each       
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.                                                      
          Some of the local memory accesses are due to register spilling                                                
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#variable-memory-space-specifiers),          
          accounting for 0.40% of the local memory load (LDL) and 9.52% of the local store (STL) instructions. 9.80%    
          of all local loads and 56.03% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 70.61% of all       
          sectors requested in L2. The local memory accesses of this workload amount to 11.02% of all executed          
          instructions.                                                                                                 
          One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being    
          indexed using compile time constants (see the "Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide            
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice    
          on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation                                         
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-hw-memory).

    OPT   Est. Local Speedup: 44.54%                                                                                    
          Every scheduler is capable of issuing one instruction per cycle, but for this workload each scheduler only    
          issues an instruction every 2.7 cycles. This might leave hardware resources underutilized and may lead to     
          less optimal performance. Out of the maximum of 12 warps per scheduler, this workload allocates an average    
          of 1.98 active warps per scheduler, but only an average of 0.46 warps were eligible per cycle. Eligible       
          warps are the subset of active warps that are ready to issue their next instruction. Every cycle with no      
          eligible warp results in no instruction being issued and the issue slot remains unused. To increase the       
          number of eligible warps, avoid possible load imbalances due to highly different execution durations per      
          warp. Reducing stalls indicated on the Warp State Statistics and Source Counters sections can help, too.

          This workload accesses local memory                                                                           
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          2.95% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each        
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.                                                      
          18.09% of all local loads and 98.91% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 18.18% of    
          all sectors requested in L2.                                                                                  
          One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being    
          indexed using compile time constants (see the "Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide            
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice    
          on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation                                         
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-hw-memory).

          to 7.8 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.       
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

          thread completion, and divergent flow control can significantly lower the number of active threads in a warp  
          per cycle. This workload achieves an average of 25.1 threads being active per cycle. This is further reduced  
          to 23.1 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.      
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

    OPT   Est. Local Speedup: 44.19%                                                                                    
          Every scheduler is capable of issuing one instruction per cycle, but for this workload each scheduler only    
          issues an instruction every 1.8 cycles. This might leave hardware resources underutilized and may lead to     
          less optimal performance. Out of the maximum of 12 warps per scheduler, this workload allocates an average    
          of 9.76 active warps per scheduler, but only an average of 1.92 warps were eligible per cycle. Eligible       
          warps are the subset of active warps that are ready to issue their next instruction. Every cycle with no      
          eligible warp results in no instruction being issued and the issue slot remains unused. To increase the       
          number of eligible warps, avoid possible load imbalances due to highly different execution durations per      
          warp. Reducing stalls indicated on the Warp State Statistics and Source Counters sections can help, too.

          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          56.99% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each       
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.                                                      
          Some of the local memory accesses are due to register spilling                                                
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#variable-memory-space-specifiers),          
          accounting for 0.46% of the local memory load (LDL) and 10.86% of the local store (STL) instructions. 10.03%  
          of all local loads and 56.78% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 71.14% of all       
          sectors requested in L2. The local memory accesses of this workload amount to 11.02% of all executed          
          instructions.                                                                                                 
          One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being    
          indexed using compile time constants (see the "Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide            
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice    
          on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation                                         
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-hw-memory).

          thread completion, and divergent flow control can significantly lower the number of active threads in a warp  
          per cycle. This workload achieves an average of 13.4 threads being active per cycle. This is further reduced  
          to 12.6 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.      
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

    OPT   Est. Speedup: 34.48%                                                                                          
          On average, each warp of this workload spends 17.6 cycles being stalled waiting for an immediate constant     
          cache (IMC) miss. A read from constant memory costs one memory read from device memory only on a cache miss;  
          otherwise, it just costs one read from the constant cache. Accesses to different addresses by threads within  
          a warp are serialized, thus the cost scales linearly with the number of unique addresses read by all threads  
          within a warp. As such, the constant cache is best when threads in the same warp access only a few distinct   
          locations. If all threads of a warp access the same location, then constant memory can be as fast as a        
          register access. This stall type represents about 34.5% of the total average of 50.9 cycles between issuing   
          two instructions.

          This workload accesses local memory                                                                           
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          57.46% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each       
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.                                                      
          Some of the local memory accesses are due to register spilling                                                
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#variable-memory-space-specifiers),          
          accounting for 0.40% of the local memory load (LDL) and 9.47% of the local store (STL) instructions. 9.86%    
          of all local loads and 56.12% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 71.06% of all       
          sectors requested in L2. The local memory accesses of this workload amount to 11.03% of all executed          
          instructions.                                                                                                 
          One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being    
          indexed using compile time constants (see the "Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide            
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice    
          on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation                                         
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-hw-memory).
